title: Earth Arc Length Calculator: Surface Distance
description: Compute the surface arc length between two angles with the Earth Arc Length Calculator — degrees or radians in, kilometres and miles out. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 45-degree arc of the Earth's surface runs 5,003.8 km — one eighth of the way around the planet, from the equator to the pole is exactly two of those.
quick_answer: The Earth Arc Length Calculator converts a central angle — in degrees or radians — into the distance travelled along the Earth's surface, the arc. Enter the angle and read kilometres or miles: the surface distance behind every 'degrees apart' statement about places, satellites and seismic waves.

Earthquake distances are quoted in degrees from the epicentre — the angle seismologists actually measure. This calculator turns those degrees into the surface kilometres the waves travelled.
A satellite's footprint and ground-station visibility are stated as Earth-central angles; arc length is what those angles mean for the people underneath.

Equator to pole is a 90° arc: 10,007.6 km. Double it for the full meridian half (180°): 20,015.1 km from pole to pole over the surface — the arc every antipode pair sits at the ends of.

body.t: New York to Boston is 306.1 km of surface — a central angle of 2.753°. Small angles, real journeys: most city pairs on Earth live inside five degrees.

popular_table.title: Arc lengths on the mean sphere (R = 6,371.01 km)
popular_table.intro: Computed as angle × π/180 × radius — the calculator's own arithmetic.
popular_table.note: These use Earth's mean radius. On the real ellipsoid a degree of latitude runs 110.574 km at the equator to 111.694 km at the poles — under 1% of variation the mean sphere smooths away.

faq: Earth's mean radius, 6,371.01 km (the IUGG value) — the standard sphere for arc geometry. Ellipsoid-exact arcs need the endpoints' latitudes and belong to geodesic tools.
Both — radians are the formula's native unit (arc = R × angle), degrees convert at π/180. Satellite and seismic literature uses degrees; mathematics uses radians.
The arc rides the surface; the chord cuts through. They differ by under 1% below about 25° of separation, then diverge — at 180° the arc is 20,015 km, the chord 12,742 km.
Because their measurements are angles: P-wave and S-wave arrival behaviour is charted against epicentral degrees. The conversion to kilometres is this page, and it depends only on the radius chosen.
The formula is radius-agnostic — enter another body's radius in a general calculator and the same arithmetic prices its arcs (the Moon's degree is about 30 km).
Arcs are taken as the positive sweep; past 180° the shorter way around is the other direction, and honest tools say which they computed.

Flights ride a few kilometres above the sphere — at cruising altitude the arc grows by roughly the altitude's fraction (about 0.2% at 11 km), a correction pilots' systems make and this page's surface framing states.
